reason: Refuted as proposed. The line is almost certainly Edson's, but the card does not meet the standard. (1) Wording: no one opened the named edition. The Faber 1999 scans on archive.org (witplay00edso, wit00marg) are lending items, and their search inside endpoint returns Item not available, so I could not open them either. Secondary sources disagree on the second sentence. LitCharts (character page) and Lavelle Porter's essay Against the Sentimental Humanities: Reading Wit (2015) give It is very simple really. Note and Query (2014) gives ‘. . . Very simple, really.’ and a Goodreads entry gives Very simple, really. The second form may come from the 2001 HBO film script, but I could not confirm that, because IMDb's quotes page returned 403. A study guide is not a named edition, so the card's wording rests on no page. (2) Locator: the page numbers the card prints are unconfirmed, and they conflict. The LitCharts character page says Page 14, the LitCharts quotes page says 14 to 15 for a longer excerpt, and StageAgent says the Ashford monologue is Faber 1999, pp. 13 to 14. Printing pp. 14 to 15 is exactly the confident false citation the rule forbids. (3) The source misuses attributed. Nobody doubts Edson wrote the line, and the note even says The line is Edson's. What is in doubt is the wording and the page, so attributed tells the reader the wrong thing, and attributed: with a colon inside the source is not the house form. Other checks pass. shipped.js finds nothing shipped and nothing near; Edson is at 0 of 3; not banned. Faber 1999 is just inside the before 2000 rule. The tag Drama is right and the speaker is named. The em dashes are inside Edson's own sentence and are allowed there. Publishable, although the play is set on a cancer ward. What would rescue it: someone opens a physical or borrowable Faber 1999 copy, confirms It is very simple really. and the page, and then ships with the citation below plus the page read. Without that it can only ride as a HEDGE, and the note must name the variant and say that no page was opened. It must not print a page range.
betterCitation: Margaret Edson, Wit, the flashback on Death be not proud (E. M. Ashford) (Faber and Faber, 1999)
